To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the antibiotic susceptibility patterns of S. aureusbiofilms isolated from DFI are significantly different from those of planktonic cells; (2) biofilms are resistant to high concentrations of the antibiotics used for the treatment of DFI; (3) ceftaroline and, to a lesser extent, gentamicin, are the only antibiotics able to eradicate S. aureusbiosfilms at concentrations achievable in vivo.

(1) biofilm formation is an important virulence trait of Staphyloccocus aureus, (2) S. aureus is the main pathogen in diabetic foot infections (3) S. aureu s is frequently resistant to the most common antimicrobials used in treating DFI

biofilm formation is a major problem in diabetic foot infections, which are often caused by methicillin-resistant strains of Staphyloccus aureus, and that the antibiotic susceptibility of biofilms is very high, which may explain the high failure rate of monotherapy in treating diabetic foot infection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new therapeutic strategy for the treatment of diabetic foot infections.

the identification of the genetic determinants of resistance and biofilm production in S. aureus isolates and the determination of antibiotic susceptibility patterns of these strains in planktonic and biofilm forms.

the development of a novel approach for the diagnosis of diabetic foot infections, based on the analysis of the antimicrobial resistance patterns of S. aureusbiofilm-producing strains isolated from diabetic patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
biofilm formation is an important virulence mechanism of S. aureu s and that biofilm infections are very difficult to treat.
biofilms should not be considered as an additional factor in the susceptibility testing, but as an independent factor in itself.

the antibiotic susceptibility pattern cannot be applied to established biofilms and that the selection of antimicrobial therapy should aim at overcoming the biofilm disease in diabetic foot infections in order to optimize clinical outcome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of ceftaroline and/or gentamicin should be considered in DFI caused by biofilm-producing S aureus strains.
biofilm formation is a key virulence factor in the pathogenicity of S. aureu s and that the susceptibility patterns of biofilms are different to the planktonic cells.
biofilm infections are difficult to treat with the currently available antibiotics, but ceftaroline and/or gentamicin may be useful in the management of these infections.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ceftaroline and, to a lesser extent, gentamicin may be considered as the first-line antibiotics to treat biofilm infections.
ceftaroline and aminoglycosides are the most promising agents in treating biofilm-related infections.
, in the case of biofilm infections, antibiotic concentrations must be increased to achieve a successful treatment.
